name: Hash Tables and Their Worst Case
intent: Understand why a hash table lookup is O(1) on average, what that average depends on (a good hash function and a bounded load factor), and how it degrades to O(n) when many keys land in the same place, by accident or on purpose.
scenario: A web endpoint parses a request with 10,000 fields into a hash map. With a good hash function and 16,384 buckets that takes about 16,000 key comparisons. If the hash function only looks at the last digit of the key it takes about 10,000,000. If an attacker who knows the hash function picks the keys, it takes 100,000,000: the same request, about 6,000 times more CPU, from one small POST.
problem: A hash table is sold as O(1) lookup, and that is true on average. The guarantee is conditional: keys must spread evenly across buckets, and the table must not be too full. When they do not, many keys share a bucket, a lookup walks a long chain or probe sequence, and the cost becomes O(n). Developers who treat O(1) as unconditional ship hash functions that cluster, tables that never resize, keys that change after insertion, and endpoints that let strangers choose the keys.

howItWorks.title: Hash, then pick a bucket
howItWorks.text: The table keeps an array of buckets. To store or find a key, it computes a hash (a number derived from the key), reduces it to a bucket index, and looks only in that bucket. If keys are spread evenly, each bucket holds few of them, so the work does not depend on the total number of keys. That is the whole reason for the average O(1).

howItWorks.title: Collisions: chaining or open addressing
howItWorks.text: Two keys can share a bucket (a collision), and with more keys than buckets some must. Chaining keeps a small list in each bucket and walks it. Open addressing stores the key in another slot of the array found by a probe sequence (the next slot, or a computed jump) and walks that sequence. Chaining degrades smoothly as it fills. Open addressing is more cache-friendly, but it slows sharply as the table fills and needs care when deleting (tombstones).

howItWorks.title: Load factor and resizing
howItWorks.text: The load factor is keys divided by buckets. The expected chain length is about the load factor, so keeping it bounded (many tables resize somewhere between about 0.5 and 1, Java's HashMap at 0.75 by default; open-addressing tables often stay lower, though some modern designs go to about 0.875) keeps lookups short. When the limit is passed the table grows, typically by doubling, and re-inserts every key. That one insert is expensive and the cost is spread over the many cheap ones, so resizing adds only O(1) amortized per insert (see amortized analysis), with a latency spike at each resize.

howItWorks.title: The worst case is real
howItWorks.text: If all n keys hash to one bucket, a chain has length n and every lookup is O(n), so building the table is O(n²). This happens by accident with a hash that ignores part of the key (the last digit, the low bits, only the first field), and with a constant hash. It also happens on purpose: if an attacker knows the hash function, they can precompute many keys with the same hash and send them (hash flooding), which turns a cheap request into a CPU-burning one.

howItWorks.title: Defences, and when to use a tree instead
howItWorks.text: Use a hash function with good mixing, and for keys that strangers control use one with a secret random seed picked at start-up, so collisions cannot be precomputed (many runtimes do this for string keys). Some implementations turn very long chains into balanced trees. When you need keys in sorted order, range queries, or a worst-case guarantee under hostile input, a balanced tree map gives O(log n) for everything, at the price of slower typical lookups and no O(1).

pros: Average O(1) lookup, insert and delete, independent of the number of keys
Simple, built into the standard library of most languages, and fast in practice thanks to compact memory layout
Amortized O(1) growth by resizing, so it can be used without knowing the size in advance
Well suited to exact-match lookups: ids, names, sets, caches, counting and grouping
cons: The O(1) is an average that depends on the hash function and the load factor, and the worst case is O(n)
No useful order: you cannot range-scan or iterate in key order, and iteration order may change between runs
Resizing pauses: one insert in a while rehashes everything, which shows up in tail latency
A table of hostile keys is a denial-of-service lever unless the hash is seeded
whenToUse: Exact lookups by key where order does not matter: sets, caches, indexes by id, counting words
Deduplication and joining in memory (see hidden complexity in loops)
Data from trusted sources, or with a seeded hash from a runtime that provides one
whenNotToUse: When you need sorted iteration, nearest-key or range queries: use a balanced tree map or a sorted structure
When keys come from untrusted users and the runtime does not randomise its hash: use a tree map, a seeded hash, or cap the number of keys
When one slow operation breaks a deadline and the resize pause cannot be pre-allocated away
pitfalls: Writing a hash function that ignores part of the key (last digit, low bits, first field): clustered keys then pile into a few buckets
Never resizing, or resizing at a high load factor: chains grow with n and the table degrades to a linked list

Accepting user-chosen keys (JSON object fields, query parameters, form fields, headers) into a hash table with a predictable hash: hash flooding makes one request cost O(n²). Seeded hashing is the usual defence, which is why some runtimes randomise their string hashes
Mutating a key after inserting it: its hash changes, so the entry sits in the wrong bucket and lookups miss it. Use immutable keys
Breaking the contract between equality and hash: two keys that compare equal must have the same hash, or the table finds neither

Floating-point keys: NaN does not equal itself under IEEE 754, and 0.0 and -0.0 compare equal while their bit patterns differ, so what a table does with them depends on the language. Avoid floats as keys
Relying on iteration order: it is unspecified in many hash tables and can differ between runs and versions
Assuming the O(1) is a guarantee under load: measure with the keys you really have, including the worst-looking ones

roles.label: Honest client
roles.description: Sends ordinary keys that the hash function spreads out.

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: Knows the hash function and sends keys chosen to collide.

roles.label: Endpoint
roles.description: Parses the request into a hash table, one insert and one lookup per key.

roles.label: Hash table
roles.description: Buckets with chains; the load factor and hash function decide the cost.

quiz.question: A chained hash table whose buckets are plain linked lists holds 10,000 keys, but its hash function returns the same value for every key. What does one lookup cost?
options: About 1 comparison, because a hash table lookup is O(1).
About 14 comparisons, since the keys are searched like a tree.
Up to 10,000 comparisons, because all keys sit in one chain.
About 100 comparisons, since the chain is split across buckets.
quiz.explanation: With one bucket holding every key, a lookup walks the chain: up to n comparisons, about 5,000 on average. The O(1) average assumes the hash spreads keys across buckets. (Some implementations, such as Java 8+ HashMap, turn long chains into trees, which is why the question says plain lists.)

quiz.question: Why do some runtimes pick a random seed for their string hash function when the process starts?
options: So an attacker cannot precompute many keys that collide, and so cannot flood a table with them.
So that lookups are faster, since random seeds mix the bits better.
So that two servers running the same program produce the same table layout.
So that resizing is never needed, since random hashes cannot collide.
quiz.explanation: With a fixed, known hash, an attacker can compute thousands of keys that land in one bucket and make each insert O(n). A secret seed means they cannot know which keys collide. Collisions still happen, but only at the ordinary rate.

quiz.question: Which need is the best reason to choose a balanced tree map over a hash table?
options: Looking up single keys as fast as possible on trusted data.
Saving memory, since a tree stores keys more compactly.
Avoiding the need for keys to be comparable or hashable.
Iterating in key order, or a worst-case bound on untrusted keys.
quiz.explanation: A balanced tree map keeps keys ordered, so range queries and sorted iteration are natural, and every operation is O(log n) in the worst case, whatever the keys. The price is slower typical lookups than a hash table and keys that must be comparable.
